opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tricky problem, because hardware design cycles are long. You're making decisions now about a chip that might not be deployed for two or three years, and then it'll be in service for several years after that. So you're trying to predict where machine learning will be maybe five or six years out, which is hard in a field that moves this fast.

The way I think about it, you want a portfolio. Most of the chip has to be solid, well-understood functionality that you know will matter for the workloads people actually run: dense matrix multiply, good memory bandwidth, a fast interconnect. Then you can carve out some smaller fraction of area or design effort for more speculative features, things that could pay off big if a certain research direction takes hold.

To decide whether a speculative feature makes the cut, a few questions matter. First, how much does it cost in area, power, and design complexity? Something cheap that could give you a big win if a trend materializes is often worth including even if you're not sure it will be used. Second, how big is the upside? If it gives a 10% improvement on some niche model, that's a hard sell. If it could make a whole class of models dramatically more efficient, say a lower-precision format or better support for sparsity, that's much more compelling. Third, do we have evidence from the research side? It really helps to have ML researchers and hardware people working closely together, so the hardware folks can see what researchers are experimenting with, and researchers can understand what's cheap or expensive to build.

There's also a nice feedback loop. If you put in a feature and it turns out to be really useful, researchers start designing models around it, and that justifies investing more in it in the next generation. If it doesn't get traction, you've lost a little area, and you learn something.

So it's really a risk-weighted bet: low-cost features with potentially large payoffs, grounded as much as possible in what's showing promise in research, while keeping the core of the design focused on what you're confident will matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long chip design cycles but does not say that larger design changes need to be introduced earlier in the design process.

r002.rationale: It endorses speculative features when their area cost is low and their potential payoff is large.

r003.rationale: It values evidence from research and researcher–hardware collaboration, but does not state that major design changes warrant careful ML experimentation to establish confidence they will work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the harder parts of the job, because the timelines are so long. If we're designing a chip today, it's going to be in production maybe two, two and a half years from now, and then it'll be the main thing people use for another three or four years after that. So you're really trying to predict what machine learning is going to look like five or six years out, and the field moves fast enough that you're going to be wrong about some things.

The way we try to approach it is a pretty tight loop between the people doing the ML research and the people doing the hardware design. We'll have a bunch of candidate features, and for each one we try to ask a few questions. One is, what fraction of the workloads we care about would actually benefit? If it helps one model that's popular right now but we don't think it generalizes, that's a weak signal. If it helps a whole class of computations, like lower-precision arithmetic did, or sparsity support, that's much more interesting. The second question is, what does it cost? Everything costs area, power, design complexity, and verification time, and those are all zero-sum on a chip. So a feature that gives you a ten percent win on a narrow set of models but takes up area that could have gone to more matrix multiply units or more memory bandwidth is often not a good trade.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is we try to actually run the experiments in software first. We'll take the proposed feature, simulate it or emulate it in the compiler and runtime, and see what happens on real models at real scale. Sometimes the theoretical gain just doesn't materialize because the bottleneck is somewhere else, like the interconnect or the host side, and you learn that cheaply before you've committed silicon to it.

The other thing I'd say is you want to leave room for things you haven't thought of. Some of the best uses of TPUs have been things we didn't anticipate when we designed them. So you don't want to over-specialize. A feature that's flexible enough to be useful for several different things you can imagine, and probably a few you can't, tends to be worth more than one that's perfectly tuned to the model of the month.

r001.rationale: The response describes long chip timelines and the need to predict future workloads, but does not say larger design changes must be addressed earlier in the design process.

r002.rationale: It weighs feature benefits against area and other costs, but does not clearly endorse speculative features specifically when their area cost is small relative to potential performance gains.

r003.rationale: It says proposed features should be simulated or emulated in software and evaluated on real models at real scale before silicon is committed, which communicates using careful ML experiments to check that a change works.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: does this make the whole system better for the workloads we expect to run? You can have a feature that looks really attractive on a small benchmark, but it takes chip area and power that you could have spent on more compute or more memory bandwidth.

So you want to look at representative workloads, model what the feature would do, and understand whether the compiler can actually take advantage of it. How much does it improve performance? What does it cost in power, area, and complexity? And how broadly useful is it?

The tricky part is that you’re designing for workloads several years out. So I’d generally favor something that supports a fairly broad set of computations over something that makes one particular model very fast. You need a compelling benefit, but also some confidence that the benefit will still matter when the chip arrives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to connect the hardware idea to the workloads you actually care about. A feature might make one particular operation dramatically faster, but if that operation accounts for a tiny fraction of the overall computation, it may not be worth the area or complexity.

So you want to look at representative workloads, model what the feature would do for end-to-end performance, and weigh that against its costs in power, chip area, and software complexity. Can the compiler actually take advantage of it? Does it help across a broad range of models, or is it very specific to one architecture?

And then there’s the challenge that you’re designing for workloads several years in the future. So I’d generally favor something that addresses a fundamental bottleneck and gives us some flexibility, rather than something that’s narrowly optimized for exactly what’s popular today.
